task.title: Fix payment client timeouts
task.description: Payment requests intermittently time out under load. Propose a fix.

proposal.summary: Implemented as configurable client changes: separate explicit timeouts, bounded connection pooling with bounded acquisition wait, idempotency-gated bounded retries with backoff and jitter, circuit-breaker isolation, and timeout/pool/retry instrumentation, validated by comparable load tests.
plan_steps: Collect current client code, pool and timeout configuration, timeout logs, and latency and pool metrics under load to establish a baseline.
Implement explicit timeouts, bounded connection pooling, idempotency-gated bounded retries, and circuit-breaker isolation behind configuration flags.
Add the specified timeout, pool, retry, and latency instrumentation.
Run unit and integration tests against delayed and failing payment-service stubs.
Run comparable baseline and post-change load tests and review timeout rate, latency, errors, and duplicate-payment counts before rollout.

claims.statement: The payment client will set separate explicit connect, read, and total request timeouts in version-controlled configuration instead of relying on library defaults.
The payment client HTTP connection pool will have an explicit finite maximum size, maximum per-route size, keep-alive setting, and bounded pool-acquisition timeout.
Retries will occur at most twice, only after connect or timeout failures, only for requests carrying an idempotency key, and will use exponential backoff with jitter.

A circuit breaker or bulkhead will isolate the payment client so sustained payment-service failures cause fast failure after a configured threshold rather than consuming all request threads waiting for timeouts.

The client will emit labeled metrics and structured logs for timeout type, pool-acquisition wait, attempt number, latency percentiles, and payment-service status, without logging credentials or full payment details.
Validation will compare baseline and post-change timeout rate, p95 and p99 latency, error rate, and duplicate-payment count under the same documented load profile.

task.title: Fix payment client timeouts
task.description: Payment requests intermittently time out under load. Propose a fix.

proposal.summary: Reuse a single explicitly configured pooled HTTP client, separate and bound all timeout types, add idempotency-gated bounded retries and a circuit breaker, and instrument pool/timeout metrics validated by before/after load tests. Evidence for the current client code, configuration, load profile, and timeout logs was not provided, so the root cause is treated as a hypothesis to verify, not an established fact.
plan_steps: Replace per-request client/connection creation with one shared pooled client (C1, C4).
externalize and set finite pool-size, connect, connection-request, and read timeouts in configuration (C2, C3).
Add bounded retries gated by Idempotency-Key and a circuit breaker (C5, C6).
Add pool, latency, timeout-type, retry, and breaker observability before rollout (C7).
Validate with fault injection and an identical before/after load test at production peak, then roll out behind a configuration flag so pool/timeout/retry values can be reverted without a deploy (C8).

claims.statement: A single shared pooled HTTP client instance is reused for all payment requests instead of creating a client or connection per request.
The connection pool is explicitly sized and bounded in configuration with maxTotal >= 100, maxPerRoute >= 50, and a connection-request timeout <= 500 ms, replacing any small or unbounded defaults.
Connect, connection-request, and read/socket timeouts are configured as separate named settings, each with a finite value documented in configuration.
Keep-alive is enabled and idle connections are evicted or validated before reuse according to a configured idle timeout.
Retries are attempted at most 3 times, only for transient connect errors or HTTP 502/503/504, only when an Idempotency-Key is present, with exponential backoff starting at 100 ms and full jitter.
A circuit breaker opens after >= 50% failures over a rolling window of at least 20 requests, remains open for a configured cooldown, then allows a limited half-open probe.

Metrics and structured logs record request latency, timeout type, pool wait time, active/leased connections, retry count, and circuit-breaker state, tagged without payment credentials or full card data.
Under a reproducible load test at the stated production peak request rate for 10 minutes, the timeout rate and p99 latency are measured against the pre-change baseline using the same test.

items.description: Unsupported premise: no code or configuration evidence was retrieved showing per-request client or connection creation, current library, or that a shared client is thread-safe and correctly closed on all paths. Connections can still leak if response bodies are not consumed or closed after timeouts and errors, and no leak or shutdown test is specified.

Pool thresholds maxTotal >= 100, maxPerRoute >= 50, and connection-request timeout <= 500 ms are unsupported by any calculation from peak request rate, latency, route count, instance count, or downstream connection limits. The proposal itself lists those inputs as unknown, so the values could overload the payment provider, exhaust local ports, or cause excessive pool-wait failures under bursts.

The assertion that any small or unbounded defaults are being replaced contradicts the stated uncertainty about the current HTTP client library, its defaults, and its current configured values because no current defaults were provided.

No finite connect or read/socket values are specified, no valid ranges or startup validation are defined, and no total request deadline is set. Combined with retries, the worst-case attempt duration could exceed caller or gateway deadlines. DNS timeout is also listed as a possible timeout type but is not separately bounded.

Keep-alive behavior is underspecified: no idle timeout value, validation interval, eviction cadence, or comparison with the downstream server keep-alive timeout is provided. No stale or half-closed connection test or fault-injection case is specified, so reused stale connections could increase errors.

Presence of an Idempotency-Key does not by itself prove the downstream payment service deduplicates by that key, nor are key scope, expiry, payload binding, or duplicate-payment tests specified. Retrying HTTP 502/503/504 after a request may have been processed therefore creates a duplicate-charge risk if downstream support is absent or partial.

Retry semantics are ambiguous and incomplete: 'at most 3 times' does not distinguish total attempts from retries, exponential backoff has no maximum cap, and there is no Retry-After handling, retry budget, or per-request deadline. At peak load, retries could multiply payment traffic several-fold and worsen the load-correlated timeouts assumed in the proposal.

Circuit-breaker behavior is underspecified: failure classes, rolling-window duration, cooldown value, half-open probe count, per-route versus global scope, and behavior across multiple application instances are not defined. A global breaker tripping at 50% over 20 requests could block healthy payment routes, while per-instance breakers could behave inconsistently.

Interaction between retries and the circuit breaker is not specified: it is unclear whether each retry counts toward the 20-request failure window, whether retries stop when the breaker opens, or how half-open probes interact with queued retries. No test covers this interaction.

The claim that metrics and logs exclude payment credentials or full card data has no supporting redaction rules or tests for URLs, headers, error bodies, exceptions, Authorization values, or Idempotency-Key values. Metric tag cardinality limits are also unspecified, creating both sensitive-data leakage and observability-cost risks.

The load-test claim references a stated production peak request rate, but no peak rate, baseline timeout rate, baseline p99 latency, downstream environment, or pass/fail thresholds are provided. Without those values, improvement or regression cannot be determined from a 10-minute test.

A 10-minute load test does not validate long-lived pool behavior such as idle eviction, stale connections, slow connection leaks, breaker recovery, or retry behavior under sustained downstream degradation. Fault injection is mentioned in the plan but is not expressed as measurable cases in this claim for connect, read, pool-wait, DNS, or downstream-processing timeouts.

Configuration-flag rollback is not reconciled with a single shared pooled client: changing pool or timeout values may require rebuilding the client, and no requirement specifies closing the old client, draining in-flight requests, or preventing duplicate clients during rollback. This creates a regression risk during the proposed no-deploy revert.

task.title: Fix payment client timeouts
task.description: Payment requests intermittently time out under load. Propose a fix.

proposal.summary: Intermittent timeouts under load are consistent with several unverified causes, including connection-pool/socket exhaustion, unbounded or mis-sized timeouts, stale pooled connections, retry amplification, and downstream saturation. This proposal makes each candidate fix separately configurable and measurable so the actual cause can be confirmed rather than assumed.
plan_steps: Collect production evidence before tuning: current client/pool/timeout/retry configuration, timeout rate and phase, p50/p95/p99 latency, connection/socket counts, DNS behavior, downstream 429/5xx rate, and peak requests per second and concurrency.
Reproduce the timeouts in staging with a load test matching the measured production peak rate, concurrency, payload mix, and duration of at least 30 minutes.
Implement claims C1-C5 behind configuration flags so pool size, timeouts, retry, bulkhead, and breaker limits can be changed or rolled back without a code deploy.

Implement observability in C6 and run the same load test at 1x and 1.5x measured peak; compare timeout rate, latency, socket count, retry amplification, and downstream error rate against the pre-change baseline.
Roll out gradually with the flags, monitoring timeout rate, payment duplication via idempotency records, downstream 429/5xx rate, and latency against the pre-change baseline.

claims.statement: Reuse one pooled HTTP client/connection pool per payment endpoint instead of creating a client/connection per request, with keep-alive enabled and max-connections-per-host set from load testing.

Bound every phase with explicit, configurable timeouts: connect timeout 2s, TLS handshake timeout 5s, and per-attempt request timeout 10s unless provider documentation or measured p99 latency requires a different value.

Set pooled connection lifetime/idle timeout below DNS TTL and server keep-alive limits, e.g. lifetime 5 minutes and idle timeout 90 seconds as starting values, so stale or DNS-moved endpoints are recycled.

Retry only transient failures (connect errors, per-attempt timeouts, HTTP 429 and 5xx) for requests carrying an Idempotency-Key, with a maximum of 3 attempts, exponential backoff starting at 100ms with full jitter, and honoring Retry-After; never retry other 4xx responses or requests without an idempotency key.

Add client-side concurrency limiting/bulkhead and a circuit breaker sized from measured downstream capacity, returning a fast, typed overload error instead of queueing until timeout when saturated or when the breaker is open.

Emit structured metrics and logs per attempt: request latency histogram, timeout count by phase, retry count, circuit-breaker state, pool in-use/idle connections, and downstream status codes, tagged by endpoint but not by sensitive payment data.

The implementation language/framework and whether the payment provider supports idempotency keys are unknown; C4 must be dropped or adapted if idempotency is not supported.

Acceptable timeout-rate and latency targets (SLOs) were not provided; the load-test target of timeout rate below 0.1% at 1x peak for 30 minutes is proposed and must be replaced with the actual SLO if one exists.
